questions.question: Which of the following statements about Serial classes is true?

options.text: They have an independent Object ID (OID) in the database.
They can be saved independently using the %Save() method.
Their data is serialized into a string and stored as a property of a %Persistent class.
They are only used for in-memory processing and disappear when the process terminates.

questions.explanation: T1.2 — Serial objects do not have an independent OID and cannot be saved independently. They are designed to be embedded within Persistent objects.

questions.question: How are properties of a %SerialObject mapped to SQL tables when embedded in a %Persistent class?

options.text: They are stored in a separate table, requiring a JOIN.
They are mapped as separate columns in the parent's table, typically prefixed with the property name.
They cannot be accessed via SQL.
They are exposed as a single JSON string column.

questions.explanation: T1.2 — The SQL projection automatically creates individual columns for each property of the Serial object within the parent's table.

questions.question: If you need to store a very large document (e.g. 5MB of text) as a property in a persistent class, which data types/classes should you avoid using?
questions.explanation: T1.2 — Both %String and %SerialObject are subject to string length limits (usually 32KB unless Long Strings are enabled). Streams must be used for large data.
